metadata.title: Claude, On Call
metadata.subtitle: The Support Plugin
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: does the support plugin answer customers on its own, or just add a queue to double-check? Lands the carry-out that Claude drafts every reply, and you decide what sends.
metadata.anchor_pair: NB05 -> NB13 (the angry three-failed-payments customer, planted as the case that breaks autopilot, paid off as the actual drafted-and-reviewed reply)
metadata.one_flag: N/A - direct mechanism description throughout (see SCRIPT.md One-flag audit)

beats.narration_text: Someone typed this and asked. Wrong verb — Claude doesn't answer support tickets, it drafts them. That's a design choice, not a limitation. So what does Claude actually do with your support queue?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Can Claude just answer my support tickets?', hesitates on 'answer', corrects to 'draft', lands the real question

props.text:

just answer my
support tickets?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('answer' -> 'draft') lands on screen.

beats.narration_text: Support is asynchronous input against a synchronous expectation — customers write anytime, and expect a reply soon. Left alone, it fragments your day into pieces too small to do real work in.

production_viz.label: THE QUEUE ARRIVES ANYTIME
production_viz.caption: if you have customers, you have support

beats.narration_text: What actually changes: reactive interrupts become batched, prioritized work. Same volume of tickets, different arrival pattern from your side. For a solo operator, that's the whole difference — a queue you process, not one that processes you.

production_viz.label: BURDEN, OR PROCESS
production_viz.caption: the whole difference, for a solo operator

beats.narration_text: For a small team, the mechanism is voice consolidation. Five people writing in five styles becomes one configured tone pulled from one shared knowledge base. You trade individual voice for consistent tone and facts on every reply.

production_viz.label: FIVE VOICES, ONE
production_viz.caption: every reply, same tone and facts

beats.narration_text: Here's the read you'd expect — full autopilot. Read the ticket, generate a reply, hit send. That's how most people picture 'AI support.' It's also the one thing this plugin explicitly refuses to do.

Here's the case the design was built around: three failed payments, two-year customer, angry. Autosend that and you risk torching the account you least want to lose. The tone-cost of being wrong is asymmetric — one bad reply here outweighs a hundred fine ones. So it doesn't send. It drafts and waits for you. That refusal is deliberate, not a missing feature.

production_viz.label: THE CUSTOMER WHO BREAKS THAT
production_viz.caption: autosend here would be wrong — so it doesn't

beats.narration_text: Under the surface, this is four narrow jobs stapled together: triage the queue, draft the replies, build a knowledge base from your history, read sentiment. That's the scope. No general intelligence — four concrete jobs the model can already do well.

production_viz.label: FOUR JOBS, ONE PLUGIN
production_viz.caption: not magic — four jobs, done well

beats.narration_text: Triage first. Each ticket gets classified into three buckets — needs you now, can wait, has a standard answer. The classifier reads features it can actually see: keywords, prior tickets, account signals. What you get back is a wall reduced to a sorted list.

production_viz.label: SORT THE WALL
production_viz.caption: the wall becomes a sorted list

beats.narration_text: Then drafting. Each reply is generated from three inputs: your configured tone, matching knowledge-base entries, and the ticket text. That mix is why it reads like a first draft, not a form letter — but the model can't tell whether it pulled the right facts for this account.

production_viz.label: DRAFT, ON-BRAND
production_viz.caption: a first draft, not a form letter

beats.narration_text: Third, sentiment. The model reads emotional tone off the ticket text and flags the frustrated and the at-risk. It's a rough signal — text doesn't always give away churn — but it beats opening tickets in arrival order. It's a router for your attention.

production_viz.label: FIND THE ONES WHO MATTER
production_viz.caption: points your attention where it's needed

beats.narration_text: It doesn't cold-start. Point it at your existing inbox and it mines what you've already answered — the same question asked five different ways — and clusters it into a structured FAQ. Your past correspondence becomes the knowledge base future drafts pull from.

Two things you configure by hand: tone — warm, efficient, or a specific blend — and escalation triggers, the words and situations that route straight to you regardless of triage. The design puts the human in the exception rule, not in the drafting loop. You define what always reaches a human; the plugin obeys.

shot.new_visual_element: SET THE TONE, SET THE TRIPWIRES

production_viz.label: SET THE TONE, SET THE TRIPWIRES
production_viz.caption: you decide what always reaches a human

beats.narration_text: In practice: hand it the overnight queue and let it group by urgency, by routine, by one-line answer. What you save isn't drafting time — that's minor — it's the context-switch tax. A morning that would otherwise stretch into two fragmented hours compresses into thirty focused minutes because you're processing one bucket at a time.

Back to the angry three-failed-payments customer. Claude drafts in your tone: acknowledges the frustration, states the payment issue, proposes a fix. You add the one line only you can add — maybe the founder called you last quarter. Then you send. The plugin caught the tone; you caught the context. That's the division of labor the design is built around.

production_viz.label: THE PLUGIN CAUGHT THE TONE
production_viz.caption: it caught the tone; you caught the context

beats.narration_text: The FAQ side compounds. Claude ranks the questions you keep answering, drafts each one, and once you publish it, that answer serves every future customer who asks. The economics flip: repeated questions get amortized instead of scaling with customer count. Recurring work, written down once.

For a live reply, the rule never relaxes: draft, review, send. Not caution — design. The plugin can't see outside the ticket: the fragile account, the exception this month, the person you already spoke to. Your review is where that context enters — skip it and you'll eventually send the reply autopilot would have gotten wrong.

production_viz.label: REVIEW, EVERY TIME
production_viz.caption: the judgment call never goes away

beats.narration_text: For the FAQ, the rule flips. Review the answer once, publish it, and it serves everyone who asks — you don't look at it again. Same drafting engine, opposite trust rule. Why? A live reply is irreversible; an FAQ page is versioned. Autonomy scales with reversibility.

production_viz.label: PUBLISH ONCE, RUNS ALONE
production_viz.caption: same drafts, a different rule once public

beats.narration_text: Claude drafts every reply — the send button is still yours. That gap isn't a bug; it's the design.

props.quote: Claude drafts every reply — the send button is still yours. That gap isn't a bug; it's the design.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I run support for a small business. Ask me the five questions my customers ask most, the tone my replies should carry, and the situations that must always reach me personally. Then draft FAQ answers for those five, a reusable reply template in my tone, and a short list of escalation triggers I should configure. Go deeper: which of those triggers should stay hard rules, and which should evolve as you watch the actual queue?
